The minimum possible value is 499.

**Setup.** Taking i = j gives |A_d| = d. If d | e, then |A_d ∩ A_e| = d = |A_d|, so A_d ⊆ A_e. Also A_e ∩ A_f has size gcd(e,f) and contains A_gcd(e,f), so A_e ∩ A_f = A_gcd(e,f).

**Structure of the sets.** For an element x, the set of divisors d of 250 with x ∈ A_d is closed upward under divisibility and closed under gcd. So it is the set of all multiples of a single divisor g, and x is "generated" by g. Let G_g be the set of elements generated by g. Then A_d is the union of G_e over e | d, so |A_d| = Σ_{e|d} |G_e| = d. Möbius inversion gives |G_g| = φ(g). The sizes are:

| g | 1 | 2 | 5 | 10 | 25 | 50 | 125 | 250 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| \|G_g\| | 1 | 1 | 4 | 4 | 20 | 20 | 100 | 100 |

This structure can be realized for all indices, for example with elements (g, r) for r coprime to g and A_i = {(g, r) : g | i}. The labeling of elements by positive integers is free.

**Optimization.** The max of A_d is the label of the last element among the groups G_e with e | d. It is best to label the elements 1 to 250 with each group occupying a contiguous block. Then max A_d is the cumulative size up to the last block among the divisors of d. So we need the block order that minimizes the sum. G_1 goes first, and max A_250 = 250 always.

For the natural order 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 50, 125, 250, the cumulative sizes are 1, 2, 6, 10, 30, 50, 150, 250. These give:

- max A_1 = 1
- max A_2 = 2
- max A_5 = 6
- max A_10 = 10
- max A_25 = 30
- max A_50 = 50
- max A_125 = 150
- max A_250 = 250

The sum is 1 + 2 + 6 + 10 + 30 + 50 + 150 + 250 = 499.

I did not check all 8! orders. I compared this order with several alternatives:

| Order | Sum |
|---|---|
| 1, 5, 2, 10, 25, 50, 125, 250 | 502 |
| 1, 5, 25, 2, 10, 50, 125, 250 | 537 |
| 1, 2, 5, 10, 25, 125, 50, 250 | worse (max A_125 = 130, max A_50 = 150) |
| 1, 5, 25, 125, 2, 10, 50, 250 | 812 |

None of these beat 499, and I did not prove that no other order does.

ANSWER: 499
